There is another thing I wish to mention in this connection. Mr. Drew, the collector of customs at the port of Morrisburg, came before the Public Accounts committee and on his oath stated that he was directed by the department of which he was an official to admit anything and everything that came in Mr. Allison's name from the United States into Canada free without examination, and without paying any customs duty. To his own knowledge boatloads and scow loads of goods came across the river-packages, cases, barrels, and crates would be piled up on the river shore on the Canadian side until a train load would be ready, when the train would come down from Morrisburg and take the goods away into the interior of the country. Our Conservative and protectionist friends are very much exercised to-day lest some goods may find their way from the United States into this country at a small customs duty. At the time I speak of they allowed their friends to import goods into Canada without paying any customs duty at all. When Mr. Drew was giving his testimony before the Public Accounts committee he was asked to produce his authority for acting in the manner described. He said it was a letter he had received from the department giving him the instructions. He was asked to produce the letter. He then said that the Commissioner of Customs of that day, Mr. John McDougald, had sent his son a little while before that to Morrisburg and had asked him for the letter and he had given it to him. Mr. McDougald was subpoenaed before the Public Accounts committee and asked to produce the letter, but he stated it had been destroyed. He was then asked to produce the copy of the letter, but said the department did not keep a copy of
it. Finally he was asked who instructed him to write the letter, and did not seem disposed to answer the question in fact he tried to refuse to answer it. He hesitated and asked the chairman if he was obliged to answer the question. Finally he stated that the minister himself dictated the letter.
Now, Sir, that is the condition of affairs that prevailed at that time. It is not pleasant for me to recall those things and I would not do it if I did not see that an effort is now being made to create a false impression in the country, and to spread the idea abroad that the men responsible for such transactions or their impenitent assigns, are the men who should be placed in charge of the public affairs of Canada. I am not aware that those men ever did penance for their crimes. They have certainly expressed no sorrow for them, and until they do I think great care should be-exercised to see that they do not get another opportunity to repeat that kind of conduct.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and his associates are very meticulous now in regard to the honour of public men. They claim that public men should be above suspicion, and that the least speck of dishonour should not attach to them. At that time, in the days I have mentioned, they were ready to swallow a camel, yea they would swallow a donkey, ears and all. They have so changed now that I imagine they would have difficulty in swallowing an oyster.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition came to the Maritime provinces last summer and visited Prince Edward Island as well as the other provinces by the sea. He made a speech in Victoria Park, Prince Edward Island to which I am going to refer, but I am sorry he is not in the House at the present moment, because I think this would be interesting to him. His speech was reported in the Charlottetown Guardian, the paper from which I have just quoted, a strong supporter of the Conservative party, having supported them right along. The right hon. gentleman commenced his speech by saying:
My idea was to try to get firsthand knowledge of this province and the other maritimes-something of the knowledge that I think I have of the other provinces of Canada.'
I will have occasion to show, I think, that he has very little knowledge regarding conditions in Prince Edward Island. Whether he has any knowledge of the other Maritime provinces I do not know. The report of his speech continues as follows-
Mr. Meighen referred to the injustice whereby two or three provinces secure special pre-war railway rates, making the commission-

That was the appeal of the leader of a great political party. That was the statement made by a man that wants to see no sectionalism in this country, who wants to see Canada become a great nation. We find him going down into the Maritime provinces and making an appeal of that kind, stating that the members of this House who supported the reduction that had been made on grain and flour last year had sold out the Maritime provinces and had given to the western men something which they should not have received.
First and foremost I want to explain to the people who may read my speech what that reduction meant. Away back in 1897 the Canadian Pacific Railway made application to the government for a sum of money to enable them to build what was known as the Crows-nest Pass railway. The government at that time agreed to the proposition, and in consideration of the sum of money that was given to the company to enable them to construct that line of railway, the company gave to the federal government a large area of coalbearing lands which they had previously received from the British Columbia government. They also made a reduction in the freight rates both east and west, which was of considerable advantage to the farmers of the prairie provinces at that time. The provinces^ were struggling then and were finding conditions difficult, and these reductions that had been made on the Canadian Pacific Railway rates were of very material advantage to them. As the years went on the Canadian Pacific reduced its rates and finally brought them, n I understand it aright, even below the rates in the arrangement made with the government. When the war came on the Canadian Pacific Railway and the other railways of Canada found it necessdry to increase their rates, and applied to the government for permission to do so, and the government of the day gave them that permission, and probably it was all right. The increase of the rates was much larger than the former rate. In order to enable them to do that the government had to suspend the operations of the Crowsnest Pass agreement. Last year that suspension and all these increases would 
automatically end, and the question was whether the suspension would be extended for another year, or whether the Crownest Pass agreement should be allowed to become effective. The arrangement made-and the Progressive party and the members from the western provinces agreed to it-was that if they got a reduction on grain and flour coming east, they would be willing to accept it and allow the suspension on the other articles enumerated on the list to remain in effect for another year. The West was working under adverse conditions. We had evidences of that from the members representing that part of the country, we knew it from the public records and we knew it from the public press. They were greatly in need of any consideration that could be extended to them and this was not a great deal. I voted for that, and I would stand upon any platform in the Dominion of Canada and justify my vote. It was for doing that that the right hon. the leader of the opposition came down to Prince Edward Island, denounced me and other members of that province and tried to raise sectional issues. Whether that is the man to be leader of a great party I have my doubts.
I want to call the attention of the House and of the public, so far as I can, to another statement which he made. The right hon. member admitted that he came to the province without having any knowledge of it, and I think he left it without having a knowledge of conditions there. The report of his speech says:
Mr. Meighen referred to the injustice whereby two or three provinces secure special pre-war railway rates, making the commission incapable of reducing other rates.
He was referring to the Railway Commission. That was simply a misstatement of fact. If he knew it to be a misstatement of fact, the matter was serious. If he did not know that, he left the Maritime provinces without knowing conditions, because as a matter of fact, the Railway Commission, last year, at the instance of the members "representing Prince Edward Island-I had the privilege of presenting the argument before the commision-very considerably reduced the railway freight rates as affecting that province. On coal transported from the mines in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to Prince Edward Island, we got a reduction of from forty to fifty cents a ton. We got a considerable reduction on grain, hay, straw, potatoes, lumber, lime, gypsum and several other articles of that kind. We got a reduction of about ten per cent on package goods. We got a considerable reduction on the internal freight, that is freight

originating and ending in Prince Edward Island. We import about 70,000 tons of coal into Prince Edward Island each year and more than half of that comes by rail. If we suppose, say, half of it comes by rail, we got a reduction of forty to fifty cents a ton on between thirty and forty thousand tons of coal, and one cun easily estimate what that will amount to. Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was referring to the very considerable reductions that had been made by the present government in the consolidated revenue fund account. Since they came into office they have also reduced the personnel of the Civil Service by 3,952 employees. These measures of retrenchment were undertaken long before the economy cry was raised throughout the country.
In the early winter we had two by-elections in the Maritime provinces, during the course of which a great deal was said by our Conservative friends, particularly by the new- and I suppose distinguished-leader of the Tory party in that section of the Dominion, the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter). The changes were rung on the loss of the rights of the Maritime provinces. Now, I would ask that gentleman, or any other hon. member, what rights had the Maritime provinces that this government have taken away? And what wrongs, if any, did the Liberal party inflict upon the Maritime provinces either in 1896 or in 1921 upon their accession to office? If any wrong has been inflicted, I should like to get a record of it. Now, I ask my hon. friends on the opposite side who made such wild statements in the Maritime provinces, what rights have we lost down there that they would give us if they came into office? This is a pertinent question.
On the other hand, I propose to give them a short list of the wrongs that were inflicted upon the Maritime provinces by the Conservative party, and I am going to speak more particularly of Prince Edward Island, because I know more about that province than I do of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. When we entered confederation we had a customs duty of 12 per cent, which gave us a sufficient revenue for all our purposes, and we had practically no debt. We had some small industries at the crossroads-blacksmiths' shops, carriage and farm implement factories, even some cloth factories; we made these things for our own use and were a happy and a fairly contented people, and our population was steadily increasing. To-day it is difficult to get a blacksmith at the crossroads to shoe a horse. In a word, none of these small factories are now in existence. The customs duties have been increased to such an extent that the things which we used to manufacture for ourselves are now made in western Quebec and throughout Ontario.
We in Prince Edward Island have to find a market for our products in the open world. New England and old England have been our best markets. We are obliged to sell many of our products in the United States, regardless of the Fordney or any other tariff, simply because we have no other place to sell them. For instance, we have to sell our potatoes there. Now, the potato crop to us is very much what the wheat crop is to the prairie provinces. We must raise potatoes because our soil and climate are well adapted for them, and the potato crop fits in well with the rotation of crops. You cannot carry on dairying successfully without growing vegetables, and we find a market for our potatoes in the southern states. When the Fordney tariff went into operation it placed us at a disadvantage of 30 cents a bushel on our potatoes. We could not sell the ordinary potatoes there any longer and our farmers were obliged to raise a superior quality of this product. We raise the potatoes for seed purposes. We have got into the markets of the southern United States and also of Cuba, and in these warm countries they have to change their seed every two years. As a matter of fact, .they get better results if they change the seed every year Now, it has been found by experience that the potatoes that come from Prince Edward Island give better results than those obtained from any other part of the North American continent. We get a price for that article that enables us to raise it at some profit and sell it in the states of the American Union in spite of the Ford-
The Address-Mr. Hughes

ney tariff. We have to sell our butter and eggs and our cheese and bacon largely in England. We export some eggs to the United States. We can sell nothing in -the provinces of Canada except a few potatoes or a little hay or oats in Nova Scotia, and we send some of these products to Newfoundland. But we are shut out from the markets of Quebec and Ontario, no matter what the transportation might be, simply for the reason that the farmers in these provinces can supply and more than supply the cities around them. Not only do they do that, but they compete with us in the small markets of Halifax, Sydney and St. John. We sell a few eggs in Montreal, but only -a few. We are bound to cultivate the markets of the world wherever we can find them, and we are forced to buy our manufactured products in Quebec and Ontario at a price which is enhanced by customs duties. That is the condition of things; and these high customs duties were placed against us by the Conservatives in this country. That is one of the disadvantages under which they put us. But there is a greater one for Which they are wholly responsible.
For years after the so-called National Policy had1 been put into force we were told that it was only an instrument to secure a reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States. The reciprocity agreement of 1854 had been abolished in 1866 and the condition was very serious in the Maritime provinces. But the people in that part of the country were willing to put up with a good deal of temporary inconvenience so long as they thought it would lead to a renewal of the reciprocal trade arrangement which we had had with the United States some time before. However, things remained' in that state for years and hope was deferred until finally in 1911 the Liberal government then in office succeeded in making a trade arrangement with the United States which was far better than anything we had ever expected. But the Conservative party in this House and in the country prevented the Canadian people from accepting the offer. No greater crime, no greater injustice could have been perpetrated, no greater disadvantage could have been placed upon the Maritime provinces. And they do not appear to be sorry for it. I heard the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) declare to-day that he was pleased that that arrangement with the United States had never been completed. It was better for the country, he said,-and in this he only repeats what other Conservatives have said hundreds of times-because the United States fMr. Hughes.]
later on would in all probability have abrogated or suspended that agreement as soon as they should have discovered that it was advantageous to Canada. How does he know that? That is only a surmise.

He knows it from past
experience.

We will examine that
point. That was immediately after the civil war had been concluded in the United States. Now, what attitude did official Great Britain take in that great crisis? I am sorry to say, as a Britisher, that the official attitude of Great Britain was directly opposed to the northern states regardless of political parties. Great Britain had shown no sympathy whatever with the northern states in that trying time.

The upper classes
showed none.

And the political classes,
too.
What about John Bright?

I will mention him in a
moment. Disraeli, Gladstone, Palmerston, Russell, Roebuck and numbers of other men whose names I cannot recall went out of their way to show their lack of friendship for the United States. Privateers were built and fitted out in Great Britain and they went to sea and preyed upon the commerce of the northern states, prolonging the struggle. Those ships never saw an American port. They were built in Great Britain, they were fitted out in Great Britain, and they were manned in Great Britain; and this, notwithstanding that Mr. Adams, the American Ambassador, had informed the government time and again of what was going on. The common people of Great Britain were suffering great privations, particularly in the cotton industry in Lancashire and Manchester owing to the stoppage of cotton imports from the United States. But, to their eternal credit, be it said that the working people of Manchester, notwithstanding their hardships, sent an enormous petition to President Lincoln wishing him godspeed in the great struggle he was making for humanity and civilization. They told him that they were willing to endure those privations; they were making no trouble, because they knew that he was striving to do what was right. That incident perhaps did more than anything else to prevent an open break between Great Britain and the United States. Lincoln was touched to the heart by it and he sent a most cordial reply to those people, because

The Address-Mr. Hughes
he was one of the people himself and he knew that their heart was in the right place. Lord Granville, Cobden and Bright were outstanding figures who took the other side, because they were men and they understood the struggle that was going on. They understood what it meant to humanity and to civilization, and when the war was over it was then, smarting under those conditions, that the United States denounced the reciprocity treaty, and we have no right whatever to assume that they would have taken similar action provided we had entered into an agreement they had made in good faith with us in 1911. That agreement was proposed by the Republican party in the United States, the party of high protection. They would not have repealed it, in all human probability, and the Democrats, the party of low duties or moderate protection, if they had come into office very likely would not have denounced it; so when our friends opposite say that it was a good thing we did not enter into that arrangement because it likely would have been denounced they have no justification for suggesting such a thing. It is only an excuse, and a weak excuse, for the crime they committed against the Canadian people on that occasion.

over the plate.

I might say a few words
on the question of the tariff. The tariff is a perennial question in this country. It has been discussed in this House for many years and I suppose it will be discussed here for many years to come. Our Conservative friends take what appears to me to be a very peculiar position in regard to this matter, but perhaps they have their reasons for doing so. A short time ago I read in the Montreal Gazette an account of a speech delivered before the Conservative Business Men's Association in Toronto by Senator Gideon D. Robertson. Senator Robertson, having been a member of the late administration, being now a senator of Canada, and speaking before the Conservative Business Men's Association, and having been warmly commended the next day by the Montreal Gazette for his speech, I presume delivered on that occasion what might be considered almost an official utterance. In passing, I think the Montreal Gazette is the sanest and most respectable English-speaking protectionist newspaper in Canada.
Your forget the celebrated weekly.

I disagree entirely with the Gazette's policy but it presents its arguments fairly; and I fully believe this, that if you see in the Montreal Gazette what is alleged to be a statement of fact you can depend upon that statement. If it quotes figures, you can depend on them; but I do not agree with its policy, and I am not impressed with its arguments. Senator Robertson in that speech made this statement:
The term "protection" may properly be applied to a variety of national activities. For example, the British navy is more of a protection to British commerce than the tariff.
I do not know what that means. Of course, I do not lay claim to any great amount of intelligence, but I suppose I have the intelligence of the man on the street. Now if the senator means that the British navy protects commerce from pirates on the high seas, I can understand that that would be a protection to commerce; but there are no pirates on the high seas now, and the navies of all the countries of the civilized world would be engaged in the same business if that is what he meant. They would keep the ocean lanes free from pirates. If he meant that the British navy imposes British goods upon the weaker nations or upon the Crown colonies at the cannon's mouth, I think he is mistaken. Great Britain herself and, so far as I know, the Crown colonies are open to the commerce of the world. There is no advantage that the British navy gives to British commerce that it does not give equally to the commerce of all the other countries of the world. It protects them all. However, that is not a very serious matter. He goes on to say:
The customs tariff serves two specific purposes. It protects home industries and the workmen employed therein, and affords a substantial part of the country's revenue.
Then he went on to make the statement, and he proved it, that Great Britain raises by her customs tariff $13.87 per head of her population, while the United States with its higher tariff, the tariff that he and other gentlemen of the Conservative party would have us copy in this country, gets a revenue of only $2.85 per head of the population-and he says that we should adopt a tariff of that kind in order to get revenue. He proves the thing that free traders have always maintained, that if you put the tariff high enough you will get no revenue at all. But the people will pay just the same. All through the senator's speech it is implied that if we adopt a tariff similar to that of the United States, we will get a larger revenue, and we can consequently do away with other forms of taxation. Of course, the senator contradicts him-

self, but his arguments are just as sound and just as logical as any arguments I have ever heard from a protectionist.
When my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) was speaking this afternoon, he referred to the importation of agricultural products and other things that we were bringing in from the United States, and when someone asked him why we were bringing these things in he replied, "Because they are cheaper there." He and others just ring the changes; they declare that if we adopt a tariff policy similar to that of the United States it will increase the price of agricultural products in this country, that is, it will raise the price to the farmer, while in the United States it appears to depress the price the farmer receives for his products. Why does the remedy act so differently just south of the international boundary line, a line that is almost invisible in some places? I cannot understand these things. I have not the intelligence of these men, I suppose; it is too intricate a question. Another thing I cannot understand is this: If the manufacturers of Canada cannot hold the home market with a moderate tariff, how in the name of common sense are they going to manufacture goods, send them into the markets of the world, meet competition there, and perhaps encounter customs duties in other countries? And yet they say they can do that. Sitting down and talking with some of my Conservative friends I have asked how that could be done and I never got an answer. I can see how it could be done in a small way, that is provided the customs duty, or the tariff, was put high enough in Canada to enable the manufacturer to have a large profit upon the goods he might sell at home and enable him to sell below cost what he might send abroad. That could be done, but would it be an advantage to Canadians? My impression is that it would be an advantage to the other fellow, the man we call the foreigner. He would be getting goods cheaper than we would be getting them, he would be getting goods below cost. My hon. friend the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) spoke yesterday afternoon. I think he is a sincere protectionist, an honest protectionist. He was anxious to see a tariff in this country which he called "the cost of living tariff" and he was stating that when we would send our wheat, for instance to the Old Country, we would not load the ships with wheat entirely, but would load them partly with manufactured goods.
I think I will read the paragraph in question, it will serve to make my point clearer. In

reply to the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) said:
Would my hon. friend expect any country to take nothing but wheat and flour from us? Would he expect a ship to be loaded with wheat and flour only? No ship will go out with such a cargo.
Then the hon. member for Springfield asked:
Why not ?	[DOT]
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said in reply:
To create a general trade we have to carry various products to other countries.
Then my hon. friend the member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) interpolated a question. He asked:
What will it bring back in return?
That was a crucial question. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George felt that, and he did the best he could under the circumstances. He said:
That is precisely the point I make with my hon. friend from Swift Current. It creates trade; but our customers overseas will not say to us that they want only our wheat and flour. It is necessary and essential for trade routes to be made up by exporting other commodities besides wheat and flour in order to create in the foreign port the needed market for our wheat and flour, because the more trade we have with any country the more demand there is for our particular product. Therefore I say we should export manufactured goods also with our wheat and flour.
Again I come back and ask, how can we export manufactured goods to Great Britain if we cannot hold the home market with moderate protection? The thing is a mathematical absurdity. No tyro in economics, in my judgment, would advocate such a policy. I think the manufacturers of Canada, and their friends, have dwelt upon that phase of the question so long that they cannot see any other side to the issue; they have come to think that they are stating sound doctrine. Was it not George III-
George IV.
Who thought he won the battle of Waterloo?
Yes, George IV.

That in the opinion of this House, a substantial reduction in the import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and-
Hear, hear.

-and is in just accord with the true ends of a protective tariff.

I heard my right hon. friend declaim last session and the session before that he never changed his policy or his principles, that the wicked men on this side of the House had done that kind of thing, but he was far above such a course. I read an article in the Montreal Star-
The whisper of death.

Yes, sometimes called the Montreal Star. It is headed "Bridging the gap", and it states that a large petition was being got up by the coal mine owners and others of Alberta and the coal consumers of Ontario, asking the government to so reduce the cost of transporting coal from the mines in Alberta to the consumers in Ontario that we could keep out American coal, and that the consumers would get cheap coal, and the petitioners went on to say, according to this article, that this would open up the mines in Alberta, give employment to a large number of miners and furnish cheap coal to the Ontario consumer, but the Star kills the whole thing in one line at the end. How about the other taxpayers who must meet the railway deficit?

I doubt it.

Well, it may increase the size of the city. It may have that result temporarily. It may do these things. But how about the consuming public who have to pay the cost. How about the general public who have to pay the bill? Somebody must pay the bill in the end. The Montreal Gazette, for which publication I have a great deal of respect, discusses quite frequently the subject of carrying grain from western Canada through the Maritime provinces, routing the grain that way and developing the ports of the Maritime provinces, and says that notwithstanding the fact that it might cost a little more to do that, the grain could be brought to Portland a little cheaper. The Montreal Gazette has frequently discussed that question, and it winds up by saying that it is bad economics because the general public would have to pay the deficit on the National Raibvay. If this is bad economics the policy of protection is bad economics, and the Montreal Gazette ably edited
The Address-Mr. Hughes

as it is, strongly advocates the one and denounces or discourages the other. I have heard our friends the protectionists state, and they had no hesitation in stating, that if we adopted a tariff policy higher than it is now, a policy somewhat similar to that which they have in the United States-although it does not seem to work very well there so far as the farmers are concerned

it would work splendidly here, it would stop emigration, would increase immigration, would give more employment, would raise wages, would raise the price of farm products, and at the same time decrease the cost of living. I think they are too modest in the advantages which they claim their tariff would accomplish. Would it not also cure earache and headache, lumbago and sciatica, remove dandruff and prevent the hair from falling out? Mrs. Lydia Pinkham's pills would be nowhere alongside an adequate tariff, which, in the estimation of these gentlemen, would be a tariff made up by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
Another argument, if it can be called an argument, that I often hear is that it is responsible for the development that has taken place in Canada. They say that a few years ago we were a smaller country than we are now, that we manufactured less, but that we are getting along better, and are developing and increasing. They point to the enormous development in the United States, and assume that it is all due to the protective tariff. That is a purely gratuitous assumption. The United States of America is an empire within itself. It has every variety of soil, climate and production. The people are most energetic and are the greatest commercial community on the face of the earth. They have prospered in spite of protection, not in consequence of it. Canada has done the same, in spite of protection and not in consequence of it. You might as well say that because the trees bud in the spring and the brooks run to the ocean and the birds sing in the forest, that is due to protection. I do not know what claim will be made for this panacea in the future. Perhaps the dictionary has already been exhausted in mentioning all the good things that can be said. But let us come back to the facts again. We must be sensible men, and surely we can arrive at a reasonable conclusion in regard to these things. If our protectionist friends would tell us frankly that we do not want to do business with other countries; that we want to have Canada for ourselves and for ourselves alone; that we want the home market for ourselves alone, I could then understand their argument in favour of

a tariff wall being placed around Canada. But when we say that our progress, development and future depend largely on the trade we shall do with other countries throughout the world, why in the name of common sense do we proceed to fine those who endeavour to carry on that trade? Customs tariffs are after all only a fine. Nations do not trade with each other, although I heard the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) make that slip the other day. I think it was a slip. Nations do not trade with one another except in a small way. Governments may buy things from one another in time of war; but in time of peace and under all normal conditions, individuals, companies or corporations trade with one another, and it is as true as the proposition that two and two make four that individuals, companies or corporations will not engage or continue in trade unless it is to their mutual advantage to do so. If it is to the mutual advantage of individuals, companies or corporations in different countries, it follows, as the night follows the day, that it must be to the advantage of the respective countries. All trade is founded in the last analysis on barter. We must buy if we want to sell.
Mr. H. G. Wells, the noted publicist, a man well acquainted with Europe, in an article that I read the other day, stated that the curse of that part of the world was due to the fact that there were so many small countries in Europe surrounded by national tariff walls, in consequence of which it was almost impossible to carry on trade and commerce between the different nations of Europe. There were national prejudices, national tariffs, national customs, national restrictions of all kinds. These nations hobbled themselves and then they wondered why they could not walk better. Are we to imitate that kind of thing in America? I do not see any sense in the world in nations subsidizing steamers, sending trade commissioners into other countries in order to promote trade, and then, on the other hand, fining the men who engage in the trade, trying to stop them; with one hand trying to promote trade, and with the other trying to stop or impede it. WTe ought to be sensible, logical, or at least endeavour to be logical. If we do ' not want the
9 p.m. trade of other countries, let us say so and confine ourselves entirely to Canada. The protectionists do not go that far; they do not want to go that far, because that would be ridiculous. They seem to imagine that there is something in that old

The Address-Mr. Hughes
dictum attributed to Barnum that a number of people are standing around all the time waiting for somebody to fool them. I hope the Canadian people will not be fooled.
Another statement that I was nearly forgetting, we hear from our protectionist friends. They deplore class consciousness in this country. They are sorry that the farmers of western Canada have grouped themselves together to promote their own interests. We have no room, they say, for that kind of thing in this country. There should not be any classes-except the Canadian manufacturers! They can monopolize that field. I am glad that the farmers are class conscious. They have some class interest and I do not blame them for it. I do not think they have much, because in a general way they do not want to place burdens on the other fellow in order to relieve themselves. They object, however, to being made to carry burdens foT the benefit of others, and I do not blame them for that. But before the rise of the Farmers' party, the farmers in this Canada of ours could be divided. It may be possible still to divide them between Liberals and Conservatives, but it will not be so easy. The Protectionist party is a well organized party. They have the money, and I will admit that they have a good deal of intelligence and a good deal of craft.
They do not show any of the intelligence.

They show that unfortunate principle that is with most of us, born with us, perhaps; they show a good deal of selfishness. And when elections come around, the unorganized people are largely at the mercy of the organized even though the latter group be much smaller. That is the way in which they hope to gain their victories, and they may succeed because it is no small group. We have an enemy that we cannot afford to despise. In the beginning of this protectionist business-and my memory goes back as far as 1878-it was then the infant industries that we were going to protect. Poor little things! They wanted only a nursing bottle for a year or two and it would be all right. They would return more favours than they had ever received when they would grow up to be big, strong, lusty men. A good many farmers were caught. The unsophisticated farmers will be caught by that kind of thing. I saw a cartoon somewhere that hits that off pretty well. The protectionist has just to be rocked for a year or two and to be fed carefully and tenderly until he grows to be strong, and he will return all the favours. The old farmer sat down by the cradle and he rocked and rocked.
Twenty years, twenty-five years, thirty years passed and the farmer was growing old and weary. The infant had grown to boyhood, then to manhood and had reached such giant proportions that it was very hard for the old man to rock the cradle and he complained and wanted to stop. What was the reply from the "infant"? "Old hayseed, if you stop rocking this cradle, and do any more whimpering, I shall get out and kick your damned head off". I was reminded of that cartoon by an article I saw in the Montreal Star a day or two ago. It stated that the present government had dropped two pilots, Mr. Fielding and Sir Lomer Gouin, and it referred to the historic parallel of Bismarck's dismissal by the young kaiser of that day, which led to the celebrated Punch cartoon by Tenniel entitled Dropping the Pilot. As I say, that reminded me of the other cartoon, and I thought it very appropriate.
I have endeavoured to put my views on the trade question before the House as clearly as I know how. I sometimes think that a good many of our really sane men are locked up in the insane asylums and that the mad fellows are on the outside, bungling the affairs of the world-preparing for war; creating, or not trying to assuage, national prejudices: carrying on commercial wars in a world that was made so fair and that produces an abundance for all the people whom God put upon it, if we would only agree to exchange our products with our neighbours. All we have to do is to be rational and reasonable, exchanging the things that we can produce cheaply and well for the products which the people of other nations can produce cheaper and better than we can. In this way the welfare of the whole world would be enormously increased, and this exchange of products would be in itself the greatest of industries and give employment to countless numbers of people. But we do not do that, we proceed in another way. Of course, I recognize that we in Canada cannot control the world; we have got to take conditions as we find them and do the best we can under the circumstances. For that reason I do not think we could do away altogether with customs duties or with tariff legislation; but we can show an example to the rest of the world. And I cannot imagine that a lowering of our customs duties and allowing the goods of other nations to come in will injure us to any great extent. Nobody will send us goods unless we pay for them, and we can only pay for them in kind-in products of the farm, the sea, the mine and the forest. If we pay
The Address-Mr. Bird

for them in that way, how in the name of common sense can our industries be ruined or destroyed?	[DOT]
But I am getting into the tariff question again quite unintentionally. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the House for listening to me with so much patience and attention.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with absorbing attention to the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) who has just taken his seat. It is the first refreshing utterance that we have heard from that side of the House since the hon. member for Brorne (Mr. McMaster) saw fit to move his belongings over here. In the early part of the hon. member's speech I shrank back a little when he ventured down the slopes of the Avernus of political recrimination, but I was glad he did not dwell there too long, and I hope he will not venture there again because I think it was the only blot upon an otherwise welcome speech.
In his remarks with regard to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) he shed a new light upon the hon. gentleman's character. I wish he were present, for I should like to have another good, square look at him. He was described as being a sincere and honest protectionist. Therefore such a protectionist is one who believes in the Laurier-Fielding tariff. I appreciate very much the strong grasp which the hon. member for King's, P.E.I., has manifested in his speech of the history of the controversy between free trade and protection, and I think we are indebted to him for presenting it to us in an historical light.
The other day we listened to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) dealing as usual with matters of partisan interest and forgetting, I am afraid, the matters that engage the public mind of Canada at the present time. I listened to them, as I always do, with unstinted admiration for their great gifts and powers; and as I listened I could not help asking myself the question, in the manner of the very well known phrase, what has all this to do with the condition of Canada? I think that question is the one that is uppermost in the minds of the people of Canada just now. Our political leaders remind me of the gods of Homer who, on the misty heights of Olympus, belabour and scold each other, forgetting the poor grovelling mortals down below, and unheeding their trials, their struggles and their sorrows, engaged the while in brilliant but trivial recriminations. I believe that were the public of 
Canada represented here to-night, as they are to some extent, what they would wish to hear from the leaders of the House and from the more prominent members of it would be some word of insight, some word of understanding, some word of discriminating sympathy for the trials through which they are passing to-day. I believe that if, in the opening of this debate by the leaders of the government and the opposition, there had been such words of sympathy and insight expressed it would have aroused a glad response throughout the length and breadth of the land where people have been cruelly hit by hard times and by the economic conditions that have overtaken this country.
In the Speech from the Throne complacent reference is made to the bountiful harvest with which our western country has been blessed. I am. afraid, however, that the significance of that bountiful harvest has been altogether lost upon the framers of that address and also upon other members of this House, if we may judge by their contributions to this debate. A year ago members on this side of the House painted the conditions of the West in very dark colours and they were scoffed at and sneered at for so doing. But time and events have justified them, and I think it is widely conceded that their picture was only too true; and those who took the opposite view are now thrust forth like foolish prophets. In my opinion time and events have fully justified the picture as presented from this side last year; and if conditions were bad then they are a good deal worse now, and I am afraid that the bountiful crop has onfy served to intensify, in the consciousness of the farmer of the West, the real character of the economic injustices under which he labours. There is a phrase that occurs in the famous Chartist Manifesto in reference to a similar situation, and I think it hits off the present condition quite well. I think it is the closing sentence which says:
Once more the foolishness of our rulers hath made the goodness of God of none effect.
That is true of conditions in the West at the present time. The good crop which has come from the bounty of Providence is like the spotlight: it has but deepened the surrounding shadows in the consciousness of western farmers. In days gone by good times have followed bad times and the farmer has been led to forget his troubles. But I doubt whether he is going to forget any more. I think the iron of circumstances has burnt into his soul so deep that from this time forth he is not going to forget. The seven fat kine may swallow up the seven lean kine,

The Address-Mr. Bird
but the farmer will not be misled. I believe that the farmer of the West and the farmers throughout Canada, by reason of Nature's bounty last year, will begin to study causes and not effects; they will become, as they are becoming, in a startling fashion which I could describe if I had time, radicals in the truest sense of the word, and are divining, with a clearness and precision which they have never indicated before, the true causes of their periodical misfortune.
I will not go detail by detail over the Speech from the Throne, but probably I shall serve a better purpose by presenting to the House as I see it the economic situation in which the farmer is struggling. If I were to analyze the condition of the Canadian farmer it would be in this manner: I would inquire into the matter from the point of view of the remedial measures that should apply. There are certain things which the farmer can do for himself; the remedy is largely within his own power. There are certain other things which the farmer can do only through organization and co-operation in association with his fellow farmers. But there are other things that the farmer can only accomplish through the sympathy and the co-operation of governments, and they form no small part of the farmer's problem at the present time.
Now with respect to these things which the farmer controls himself, they relate largely to the technical side of his profession, and include all those improvements he may introduce into his operations as an agriculturist. We all know what they are, because it is quite the vogue nowadays to press those things upon the farmer-the eradication of weeds, the conservation of the soil, the rotation of crops, the mixing of his operations, and so on; we are all familiar with that, it is the favourite remedy prescribed by the farmer's city friends. They are very fond of saying:	Now there you are; go to
it; there is the whole secret of your trouble, you do not know how to farm. Occasionally a general manager of a bank, a railway magnate, or a representative of big business, and sometimes a cabinet minister, will leave his highly polished office in the city and take a flying trip through rural Canada I notice that the poetic instincts of these gentlemen never fail to be impressed by the wide expanse of growing grain undulating in the glorious sunshine of the West, but at the same time they never fail to be impressed by the slovenly and inefficient manner in which the farmer is trying to make ends meet. I came across a gentleman of that kind when coming down to Ottawa He blamed the
farmer's economic troubles upon the farmer himself. The farmer was inefficient,, incapable, disorderly, and I forget just what other adjectives he used; but behind that man's loud and blatant arraignment of the farmer I saw as I nearly always do see, an impenetrable wall of ignorance as to the actual conditions under which the farmer lives. There are quite a number of people who are not ignorant, or who should not be, who often by implication make practically the same charge against the farmer. Even the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) seems to trace all the troubles of the farmer to that cause- he is farming wrong, unscientifically.
The idea for the western farmer is to have a small farm, well-tilled, of not more than eighty acres. I read somewhere, where weeds were absolutely extinct, where everything was paradisiacal, where there was nothing that was not absolutely scientific; that is the secret of the farmers' emancipation; let him get down to mixed farming and all things will be well. Now there is nothing in the world that exasperates the average farmer more than talk of that kind, and the reason is plain. He is not lacking in modesty to the extent that he believes his method of farming is perfect. The farmer, as I know him in the West at all events is human and participates in all the weaknesses of our common humanity. Like the rest of us' he has a long way to go before he reaches perfection in his particular calling. But to say to the farmer at the present juncture, when he is up against it, when he is struggling for existence: You must change your methods of farming, those traditional methods into which you have entered after years of experience; you must change that or there is no hope for you-to speak like that to the farmer is about the same as offering a gilt-edged menu card to a starving man and saying: Now, eat, drink and be filled, and everything will be all right.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the average farmer is more willing to bring his methods up to date than sometimes governments are willing to help him. I noticed in the papers some time ago that the farmers of Manitoba were anxious to go in for mixed farming. At last the voice that had emanated from the city office had taken effect, and the Manitoba farmers really had a desire to go into mixed farming; so they sent word down to Ottawa to see if perchance they might import milch cows from Wisconsin free of duty. But I understand from the newspapers that they were politely but firmly told that it was not desirable to import American milch cows
The Address-Mr. Bird

free of duty, even though it would help in mixed farming
Then again I understand that the axe of economy, this new-found enthusiasm, this opportunist zeal for economy is going to fall first-where? Why, upon the annual grant that this government has made for the last ten years for the agriculture extension service. And yet t'he city man will go on saying that mixed farming is the cure, that nothing else is of any use whatever; so hang on to that for it will save you.
Did not the leader of the hon. member's party intimate to this House the other night that diversified farming would help to a degree?

Is not that just what I was admitting myself, that the farmer has a sufficient degree of intelligence to admit that diversified farming is desirable? Let me tell my hon. friend that diversified farming will come as soon as the antecedent conditions that are necessary are brought about, as soon as governments show the necessary sympathy and co-operate. I want to interject here that farming as an occupation is carried on by numerous people in this country who are the descendants of people who carried on farming before them, and that being the case the traditional rules of their, vocation have arrived at a consensus. There is an accumulated wisdom in the farming profession of this country which may not be quite as high as it ought to be. but I venture to say that this accumulated wisdom that resides within the average farmer of this country is superior to anything that can be offered to him from any office chair or from any college professor.
Let me pass on to the second series of cases I have in mind. Now, there are things which the farmer can do through organization, and I am glad to think that the co-operative spirit is taking so strong possession of the farmer of Canada. If there is one thing more significant than another in the rural life of Canada to-day it is the quick growth of the co-operative spirit amongst farmers, especially out West, during this last year or two. It is spreading through the West almost like a gospel, and is capturing the imagination and the mind of the farmer, and there is very little in the farmer's mind at the present time that weighs equally with it.
Two sessions ago when the organized farmers made representations here to this parliament for a wheat board they were met with very strong and very insistent opposition right in this place, and that opposition 
was so strong that the measure could not get 1 through the House until it had been debilitated by compromises that rendered it practically worthless. The farmer took it back West with him and tried to make some use of it and when he failed, as he inevitably did fail, he turned his mind in the direction of co-operative effort, and that is where his mind has been ever since. When the wheat board legislation was passing through this House the opponents of it said to the farmer "Now, it will be your salvation if you will learn to cultivate a little bit more self help. You are dependent upon governments too much. Why don't you go back and help yourselves?" But I find that the same people who opposed the wheat board and offered that advice are the very people who are trying to hamper the co-operative efforts of the farmers now. It amounts to this, Mr. Speaker: That every time the farmers of this country-or of any country for that matter -try to lift themselves up above themselves, they at once clash with some vested interest or another.
Now, as I said, the matter of co-operative marketing is a burning question in the West at the present time, and the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion, has the opportunity of its life, it has the opportunity right now to show that it is behind the farmer.
I know that the Department of Agriculture has carried on educative work for some time along co-operative lines. I read a pamphlet and a very good pamphlet, the other day on co-operative marketing in eggs. But what are eggs compared with wheat? There is a hint for the Department of Agriculture. There is a movement in the West that has for its objective the marketing of the western crop through the farmer's own self controlled channels. There is an opportunity for the government to show its sympathy for the farmer, there is an opportunity not only by lending its machinery for educative purposes, but if possible of getting behind the movement with some financial backing too. A short time ago there was a deputation of farmers here from the West Who had the audacity to ask the government for some of their own money in order to help them to organize for co-operative marketing of their wheat. I do not know, except from the newspapers, the effect of that interview, but I hope the result will be satisfactory to the farmer of the West in pursuing this very legitimate and very admirable aim of getting together and marketing the staple product of our western farms.

The Address-Mr. Bird
Then again there are a large number of things which the farmer cannot tackle, either single handed or through organization, except the parliament of Canada come to his help by administrative means or by legislation, and those things are most vital things that affect the farmers' position at the present moment. Co-operative marketing and the improved methods of agriculture will come in time, but it will be only in time. It will take many years to switch the western farmer over from his present methods to any other method, necessarily so. But what the farmers in the West, at any rate in my district, need is some relief now. That is what they need at the present time, they need attention; and the things from which they suffer are things entirely within the control of parliament. In fact the reason they suffer is because of the enactment of parliament, because this parliament has willed that they' should suffer in that way. It is not necessary for me to mention some of those things. There is the debt under which the farmer is labouring; there is taxation; there is the tariff; there is transportation. Every one of those factors in the cost of production is grinding the face of the farmer at the present time; and grinding the face of the farmer because this government here-I beg your pardon this parliament- wills that they should grind the face of the farmer. That is the situation under which the farmer is labouring at the present time. The economic situation of the farmer is right within the hands of this parliament, right within its hands at the present time. It is no use trying to move the responsibility over to the farmer himself or to any other outside origin. The crux of the whole situation is right within this Dominion parliament. Now, someone will say that this place, this chaste temple of national causes, ought riot to be degraded into a forum for the furtherance of class interest. This is the place where only the abstract good of all can be considered, and not the concrete good of a few. That is the position that one frequently hears put forward not only here but elsewhere-that this is not the place for a class to bring its grievances. But where else can the farmer bring his grievance, or carry his grievance, because here is the place of their origin? He is helpless if he is ruled out from bringing his grievance to the only place where he can possibly find redress.
Upon the financial difficulties under which the farmer labours at the present time I will not dwell very long, although I know that a good many farmers in the West believe that the financial side of their situation is the most important. During the war farmers 11
very often were led to invest their money, through patriotic incentives, and now in the process of a few short years they are left absolutely defenceless against the rapacity of their creditors. I know large numbers of them personally, and they are most sober, capable farmers, Canadian-born, who have lost all that they had accumulated as a result of their life's toil. There are many others who, though not losing all, have been saddled with a debt that will embitter their lives as long as they live. Perhaps if I were challenged to say just how parliament could help that situation I might not be able very clearly at the moment to say; but surely parliament exists for the very purpose of seeing that that kind of thing does not happen, or if it does happen that some relief can be found. During this debate an attempt has been made to show that the war was not paid for as it proceeded. We know it was not paid for as it proceeded, but it is being paid for at the present time, to the ruination of many hard working honest farmers throughout the length and breadth of this country. Talking about capital levy, I know farmers who have suffered a capital levy. Some of them have lost four, five, six or eight thousand dollars in the course of a short time, and why? Because a war occurred in which the whole nation was involved, which was the means, not of impoverishing the nation as a whole, but simply the means of transferring millions of dollars of wealth from one part of the nation to another, and is this parliament not the place to come and lay a grievance of that kind? Surely this is the place to present it because the whole financial system of this country hinges right on this Chamber.
As I said before, I have no suggestion to make as to how the government should come to the relief of victims of our financial system. Probably if I were to venture one suggestion I would be classified amongst the theorists. Last session in the Banking committee room we had a professor from a noted American university standing before us, telling us that the war had been the means of transferring wealth, without any equivalent, from one set of persons to another set of persons to the amount of billions of dollars. I think it was said to be forty billion dollars in the United States. The same thing has occurred in Canada. There are thousands of people in Canada to-day who took homesteads in the West twenty or thirty years ago, who ever since have been working hard, saving and improving their farms, and who to-day are without farms at all. I travelled to Winnipeg

with one farmer the other day who was coming down to see his wife in the General Hospital in that city. He told me that when he stood in the bank the other day and was told by the manager that the decision had been made to close him out, he felt as though it would have been as well if that manager had come and knocked him on the head. Dealing for a moment with the question of the tariff: I have listened with a great deal of interest to that subject of never failing interest; and I believe that the farmer especially in the West, will continue to be a free trader so long as he has to sell his surplus produce on a foreign market and produce those goods under conditions of protection. It needs no prophetic gift to know just where the western farmer at any rate is going to stand on the question of free trade or protection. We have before us to-night at this stage of the debate the amendment proposed by our hon. friends to the right. As I listened to that amendment, after having listened to the previous debate, I thought to myself, now here is a new version of the mountain and the mouse. After all this fierce rumbling, booming, cracking, banging, flashing and flaring, here comes forward a mouse, a poor anaemic mouse, alas, the poor distressed agriculturist. " Cheer up Mr. Farmer, we are going to add a little to the tariff; felicitate yourself, we are going to increase the duties on your machinery; leap and shout for joy, we are going to protect you into prosperity." 
I notice that the amendment draws our attention to the exodus from Canada-that doleful subject. I wondered-and yet I did not wonder-where those people are going. Does anybody here know where they are going? They are leaving Canada. Where are they going? They are leaving the farms of Canada and they are going on to the farms of the United States.	.
Not on your life!

An hon. member here knows
more than I do, and I am glad he does because that is what I would fain believe myself. That is just where they are not going. No farmer in a country that has a medium protection would ever go and farm in a country that has a big protection, because that is where the farmers really starve. They do not quite starve in Canada; but they do actually starve in the United States, and they could not help starving. I will tell you where all these people are going. They are going into the cities of the United States, those great, big swollen parasites that suck the life-blood of the American producer. They are going to swell the numbers of the parasites. Long before Great Britain enjoyed free trade, William Cobbett, when he took his ride through rural England, described the city of London, which had grown prodigiously in the then recent years, as a wen, a wart, an unsightly and ugly protuberance growing up like a weed and sucking like a vampire the lifeblood of the nation. That is true of the American cities. They are living on the lifeblood of the American producer, the man who works in the mine, in the forest or on the sea. That is where they are going. But our friends says:	"The cities create the home
market." Let me tell you what they create- a big, wide-open mouth that swallows up the hard-earned toil of the man who works by his hands, the farmer in the wheat states, the corn states and the cotton states. Oh, there is no prosperity in rural America, but there is prosperity in urban America. That is always true of protectionist countries. It cannot help being true

It is all right for his friends to protect themselves, but it is not right for anybody else's friends to protect themselves. This parliament and this government is suffering, not

The Address-Mr. Bird
through the influence of the big interests, but through the awfully corrupt influence of the civil servants and the workingmen of this country! He said: "It would be a good thing if this building and this institution could be taken right away from that corrupting influence and all those gentle, innocent looking men whom we meet in the street and who are the servants of this country." The civil servants-they are the people who are threatening the integrity of this country, and the sooner we get this parliament.away from that atmosphere, the better it will be! I will tell the hon. gentleman that right in my constituency I have a number of sites that ivould be ideal. Only I will warrant him that they would be just about as inaccessible to his friends as to anybody else's
10	p.m. friends, and it would be a fearful tragedy if the Manufacturers' Association, like the civil servants and the poor workingmen, could not bring its influence to bear upon this parliament. I think, possibly, I have summed up in those few words, the quality, essence and quintessence of that thing that was tagged on to the end of the hon. gentleman's speech and that is called an amendment. Mark you, they are asking the government to do what a speaker, a short while ago in this debate, told them was criminal to do-that was to interfere with the tariff in the middle of a parliament. It is all right to move it up, but you must not move it down.
I come now to the question of transportation. and I would like to tell the House that in the farmer's mind, there is no factor that weighs upon him so much as transportation. Neither the tariff nor anything else figures with the farmer like transportation. If you stay to consider for a moment what it costs a farmer to send a bushel of wheat or a steer to Liverpool, or eggs or poultry or cream or anything else to the home market, you will know just how much transportation figures in the mind of the average farmer.' Two sessions ago this parliament dealt with the Crowsnest pass agreement, and that was very highly appreciated by the western farmer, although, mark you, it was not much of a con-session. It was a fragmentary piece of justice that was very quickly becoming overdue. At any rate, the farmer was grateful. Last session when the government attempted to grapple with the shipping ring on the Great Lakes, the farmer was likewise appreciative according to its degree. The failure of that attempt is just as significant to the western farmer as the injustice itself with which the attempt was made to deal. It is all very well
m
for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) to taunt the government with the failure, as he did; but I would like to tell the right hon. gentleman that when you begin to struggle with the big interests, it is not the species of government at all that matters, it is the genius. It was not because it was a Liberal government that it failed, but it was because it was a government-well, just as it was a government. Governments, hitherto, and even up to the present time, are not so constituted that they are of any great advantage when they begin to handle the big interests, because the big interests seem to have some kind of inside hold, and therefore, it is not easy for any government, such as we have known governments, to tackle those big freshwater monsters that batten and thrive upon the hard-earned toil of the western farmer, that Great Lakes' Kraken that lies in wait every fall until the crop ripens and then sinks its fangs into the vital spot of commerce and holds on. But we are willing that the government should try again, because they know by this time that it is a monopoly of a peculiarly vicious kind, and the only effective way to deal with such a monopoly is either to destroy it or take it over and use it for the advantage of the public at large.
Now, this naturally brings me to a very congenial subject

the natural outlets of western Canada to the sea. There is the crux of the whole transportation question. If Canada could develop its natural outlets to the utmost, these things might not happen; if every one of Canada's avenues to the sea were developed to the fullest extent, the strain that periodically falls upon any one of them would automatically be relieved, and the element of competition would assure to the farmer a minimum charge for the carriage of his products. My friends around me know what I am aiming at. In the Speech from the Throne there was some mention of transportation and, by implication, of its importance to the farmer. But the reference was in a form that, to the western mind, seems totally unwarranted. For years, and never more insistently than now, the West has been asking for the Hudson Bay route, and the government in the Speech from the Throne says in effect: Oh, yes, certainly; here is the Welland canal. We asked for an egg and they gave us, not a white stone -using the simile of the leader. of the opposition-but a white elephant, which is worse even than a white stone. The West has had the Hudson Bay route in its mind and imagination for over a generation. Between the years 1907 and 1917 the activi-
The Address-Mr. Bird

ties of both governments were such as to make the West believe that at last its long cherished aspirations were about to be realized. In the latter year, 1917, however, it was thought best to suspend the work on the Hudson Bay railway in the interests of national economy. The West acquiesced in that view, with the distinct understanding that when the financial condition of the Dominion warranted it the work would be resumed. That was the compact, and so for four or five years public opinion in the West in regard to this project lay dormant; but two or three years ago certain sinister signs began to appear, certain signs of opposition, certain signs that that compact was in danger of not being observed. The opposition began to assume a very bitter form, until in the fall of 1922 it culminated in an attempt at vandalism such as has scarcely ever been equalled in the history of this country. An attempt was actually made not only to deface, lout even to obliterate, the work which had already been done. I am not blaming the government for it. The thing was done unknown to the public, it was done, I venture to say, without the knowledge of the government as to its real significance, and in the West there is a firm conviction that it originated in the minds of the enemies of the proposition.
That was in the fall of 1922. By that one act public opinion in the West was aroused to fever pitch. The long cherished aspiration to which the people out there had clung was attempted to be defeated in that underhand method. The revival of public opinion in the West in regard to the Hudson Bay route coincided practically with the beginning of this parliament two years ago, and during the two sessions that have passed western representatives have done their best to present the Hudson Bay railway case to the House, as Hansard will attest. Last year our hopes were again revived by the grant of $350,000 for the continuation of the work and also by various professions made on both sides of the House, only to be dashed to the ground last summer and fall by the almost entire absence of any visible attempt to spend the money. The excuse made by the government that the vote was passed too late may be a good one, it may even be adequate-and I do not question the sincerity of the government-but I would point out that it is not the kind of excuse you can use twice; it would look a little bit faded if ever called upon to do a like service. To-day the West is looking for an early vote, an adequate vote, and a sincere vote on this matter, in spite of all this talk about economy, this opportunist economy, 
that has suddenly sprung up like a mushroon in certain quarters of the Dominion, because I tell you that to the western farmer, especially in the north of those rich provinces, the completion of the Hudson Bay railway is supreme economy. Why, if the expenditure made on the Welland canal for one year were spread over two or three years it would suffice to build the Hudson Bay railway to a point where it might be tried out and taken forever from the sphere of embittering controversy. This is not merely a business proposition that you can estimate in dollars and cents. It is a matter of profound sentiment, indefinable yet nevertheless powerful, that always grows in the consciousness of people who are isolated, as we are out West, towards their natural outlets to the wide world. You are dealing with a profound community consciousness that you cannot defeat. Mention is made in the Speech from the Throne of the everlasting problem of East and West, and we know it is a problem the solution of which is of supreme importance to the Dominion. Here is a chance for statesmanship to prove itself, to grant this generation-old aspiration of the West for its natural outlet to the sea. I venture to say that if this government will see its way clear to do that, if it will make a favourable and definite pronouncement of policy on this question, it will work a revolution in the mental attitude of the West towards the East which has become exasperated by reason of an unscrupulous propaganda that has been carried on by certain newspapers in the East.
The Hudson bay proposition will come up before this House at a later stage. My hon. friend for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) has a resolution on the order paper, and when it comes up for consideration I hope to be able with others to meet some of the arguments which during this last year have been spread broadcast throughout Canada, and especially throughout eastern Canada, in regard to this proposition. Statements, in reference to facts, that are patently false, have been scattered throughout the country by means of newspaper propaganda in order to defeat the West of this legitimate aim of theirs for the opening-up of their natural channel to the markets of the world; and when the resolution of the hon. member comes up I shall deal with these misrepresentations.
On motion of Mr. Logan the debate was adjourned.
